title: The Women Obsessed With Lindsay Clancy
excerpt: Photographs by Alexandra Howland O n one of the final days of the trial , dozens of women streamed into the back of a Plymouth, Massachusetts, courtroom, fillin
body: Photographs by Alexandra Howland O n one of the final days of the trial , dozens of women streamed into the back of a Plymouth, Massachusetts, courtroom, filling two long rows of wooden benches
They stood and watched the judge and jury take their seats

Then they strained for a view as a nurse wheeled in the defendant, Lindsay Clancy, who has admitted to strangling her three young children to death in her suburban Boston home in January 2023, before swallowing prescription pills, slashing her wrists and neck, and throwing herself out of a bedroom window headfirst

Seeing her there in a wheelchair, one woman crossed herself and whispered, “Please, God.” As an officer gaveled the court into session, others pulled out notebooks, folders, and scraps of paper. “WHY,” Marta Quijano wrote as a prosecutor called a psychiatrist to the stand. “Motivation , ” she added, starring the word as the doctor began explaining his opinion that Clancy was not in the throes of psychosis on the night of the killings, as her defense has argued, but deeply suicidal and still capable of knowing right from wrong
In the back row, a woman who had flown in from Cleveland shook her head
She had a true-crime novel in her lap and turned to a blank page at the end. “Stupid experts,” she wrote
Americans have long been obsessed with murder trials, especially those involving the primal nightmare of mothers who kill their children
The public loves to watch mothers on trial and partake in their judgment
There was Susan Smith, who had drowned her three children in a South Carolina lake and was found guilty of murder in 1995, despite having a history of trauma and sexual abuse

And there was Andrea Yates, who had drowned her five children in a bathtub and was convicted of capital murder in 2002 and then retried in 2006, when she was found not guilty by reason of insanity after witnesses testified that Yates had experienced severe postpartum psychosis and schizophrenia
The Clancy trial is now part of this sadistic American tradition, but it has also become something else for the women who have been showing up in person

It was not enough for them to watch the proceedings on television, or listen to some lawyer on YouTube, or even stand outside the courthouse wearing pink and waving signs in support of Clancy, as hundreds of women did one day earlier this month

They did not want to be outside rendering judgment; they wanted to be inside, on the third floor, sitting on the wooden benches, as close as possible, in case they could notice some detail, some gesture, some pause or expression or word that might reveal a truth they could recognize from their own experience

A jury of nine women and three men will decide in the coming days whether Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor-and-delivery nurse, is criminally responsible for killing her children or not guilty by reason of insanity

The two prosecutors have argued that the killings were the premeditated decision of an entitled and controlling woman who had been frustrated that she could not master her worsening depression and sought a way out of a life that she no longer wanted

Clancy’s defense attorney, Patrick Reddington, has cast her as a loving mother failed by a fragmented mental-health system even as she repeatedly sought help for intensifying depression, anxiety, and insomnia after giving birth to her third child. [ Read: Why Lindsay Clancy’s insanity defense might fail ] Clancy saw her psychiatrist 14 times, tried 13 different medications, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room, tried to enroll in an inpatient program, and confided to her husband that she’d had thoughts of harming her children

Defense experts testified that doctors had missed an underlying bipolar disorder and prescribed pills that made Clancy’s symptoms worse, starting a downward spiral that culminated in a rare condition called postpartum psychosis that can cause hallucinations
Clancy has said that she heard a male voice telling her to kill her children, Cora, Dawson, and Callan, on January 24, 2023
After being resuscitated following her suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed from the waist down, Clancy was handcuffed, placed under armed guard, and arraigned from her hospital bed
A judge allowed the moment to be livestreamed from the courtroom; a video screen showed her unblinking eyes above a white surgical mask

The trial itself has also been livestreamed, fueling conspiracy theories that have tended to blame the killings on Clancy’s husband or an intruder, attempting to find clarity where there is little, as many women at the trial already understood
By last Monday, they were waiting in an hour-long line to get into the courthouse, and another that stretched down a bright hallway to the courtroom doors

Alexandra Howland for The Atlantic A crowd of mostly women waits in line to get inside the courthouse. “I can’t imagine what’s going through her head,” one woman was saying to her friend. “It’s not just cold-blooded murder,” the friend said. “I had suicidal thoughts, clear as a bell,” a retired teacher named Dottie Kiley told another woman in line, explaining her experience with antidepressants. “So bad I called the police and told them, and they had a cop come down and sit with me
It was a small town, and they had time to do that.” The woman behind her nodded. “She could be any one of us,” she said as the courtroom doors opened

I nside, the women listened to Avram Mack , a psychiatrist and prosecution witness, explain his clinical opinion that Clancy, having made up her mind to kill herself, then made the decision to kill her children to prevent their suffering a life without her—a theory called “altruistic filicide.” Quijano leaned over to the woman sitting next to her. “What is the validity of this three years later?” she whispered, shaking her head

After the morning break, she stood in line again for the afternoon session. “With my first daughter, because it was so difficult breastfeeding, I had insomnia and anxiety—I was worried the baby is hungry,” Quijano told a woman she had just met. “I remember one time—she was a cranky baby—and I remember not so much shaking her but going like this,” she said, demonstrating how she squeezed her daughter’s shoulders and screamed. “They are called intrusive thoughts because your brain says something, and you don’t recognize it.” Ashlyn Rizzo, who’d been attending the trial for two weeks straight, nodded. “I had been planning to run away,” Rizzo said, referring to a moment after her first child was born. “I liquidated all my 401(k) and squirreled the money away
I figured everyone was better off without me

I wrote a note.” “My cousin had a plan,” Quijano said, not needing to finish. “I was just going to start driving,” Rizzo continued. “Stay in hotels.” As it happened, Rizzo said, she had called her psychiatrist, who that very day got her into the same specialized program in Rhode Island that had rejected Clancy one month before she killed her children. “Saved my life,” Rizzo said
Alexandra Rose Howland for The Atlantic A second courtroom was made available to accommodate the large crowds
Alexandra Rose Howland for The Atlantic A woman waits outside the courthouse
Alexandra Howland for The Atlantic Kerri-Ann, a therapist, sits outside the courthouse, discussing the case with Sheila Sullivan, who researches postpartum health
Alexandra Howland for The Atlantic Kerri-Ann took extensive notes during the trial
On Tuesday, the line was longer. “I wonder, what does justice look like in this case?” a retired teacher named Lisa was saying
She had been keeping the livestream of the trial on in the background of her daily life all month, until she decided to come to see it for herself

She had driven up from Virginia. “My daughter had a moment,” Lisa, who didn’t give her last name, told the woman standing behind her, referring to postpartum depression. “I’ve been there, trying to get psychiatric appointments.” “I had a miscarriage in the second trimester and drifted into depression,” Sheila Sullivan replied, explaining that she’d wound up committed to a psychiatric facility in the 1970s. “They gave me shock treatment

Back then, they didn’t know.” “I’m sorry,” Lisa said, hugging her. “Thank you,” Sullivan said. “They don’t do any research on how hormones affect mental health,” Lisa said. “She didn’t have any symptoms until they put her on the drugs,” Sullivan said. “It’s all interconnected,” Lisa said as the courtroom doors opened and the women filled the back benches. [ Read: Pregnant and depressed ] “Can you tell us what peritraumatic disassociation is?” a prosecutor asked an FBI forensic psychiatrist, Gregory Saathoff. “It’s when you feel things are unreal, not you—like you’re watching yourself,” Saathoff began
A woman wrote down, “Witness staring at jury,” and whispered, “I think that’s weird.” Sullivan took out her notebook. “Moral judgement??” she wrote

She listened as Reddington, the defense attorney, questioned Saathoff, going through his 75-page résumé and pointing out that he had treated only two women with postpartum depression, and that that had been decades ago

Reddington went over the times that Clancy had described feeling “like a zombie” and had been in a “disassociated state,” and asked why health-care providers had not asked more questions when Clancy indicated that she was suicidal. “She was trying hard to get help,” the doctor acknowledged. “I can relate to all of this,” Jodi Fournier said as she stood in line later that afternoon. “Not at the extreme, but I can understand.” For several days, she had been driving to court with two friends from a town 30 minutes away. “The other thing is, when you work in health care, you learn not to trust the doctors,” her friend Susan Hatfield said. “She was questioning her doctors

She didn’t trust them, and neither did I.” “See that woman over there?” Fournier said, noticing a blond woman standing by herself and praying at a window outside the courtroom. “She’s does it every day,” Hatfield said

title: The Recalled-Food Show With RFK Jr.
excerpt: Hi! I am your Senate-confirmed secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F
body: Hi! I am your Senate-confirmed secretary of Health and Human Services, Robert F
Kennedy Jr., and don’t worry, the worm in my brain has been dead for a long time
Forget The Real Food Show , the cooking show that I really do host on HHS.gov
Welcome to The Recalled-Food Show , the cooking show America deserves
Summer is coming to an end! When I think of summer food, I think about having your falcon bring you a roadkill slider, but I’m told others think salad and blueberries

So I thought I would share one of my favorite recipes from the new upside-down food pyramid. (The honored top, of course, is microbes .) Someone said, “There is no sauce like hunger.” I say, “There is no sauce like the potential risk of a deadly foodborne disease.” And you can see that in my past eating habits
I’ve gone on the record saying that the only three things I won’t eat are monkey, dog, and human meat ! Obviously, I am not directly responsible for all the recalls this summer

I did wish on a monkey’s paw (shortly before sticking said monkey’s paw in my animal-parts fridge for closer observation) that all consumers of fast food would be punished, but salmonella jalapeños at Chipotle was not what I had in mind. (I was thinking more that I would wrestle these fast-food consumers individually into submission while wearing my stiffest pair of athletic jeans.) We can all agree that for too long we have been weak and coddled
Kids don’t have to fight measles and polio to earn the right to grow up, as we used to
It makes me sick (an enviable state) when I think of it
I’m working hard to rightsize the new generation with all my vaccine initiatives
So I’m grateful that food is dangerous again
Danger is exciting! It used to be that a man was a hunter
He would go out with his spear and come back covered in blood, carrying a room-temperature animal carcass
Death was on the line! When we faced the risk of death with every meal, we were probably the healthiest we’d ever been, those of us who survived
Now, to the recipe! Before this summer’s developments with lettuce, I would never touch salad
I don’t eat anything that isn’t capable of killing me; it doesn’t feel sporting
But now I eat it all the time! Finally, a worthy opponent
If you share my attitude toward risk, you’ll love this recipe! The perfect salad to end your summer

Worthy Opponent Salad Ingredients: One head of recalled lettuce One cup recalled alfalfa sprouts One cup recalled frozen blueberries One heaping tablespoon recalled lactation granola Recalled ground beef, to taste Instructions 1
Pour them into a bowl (ideally one you have carved yourself from a whale’s pelvis). 4
Sprinkle with ground beef (I like mine raw). 6
Say, “You are a worthy opponent, and may the best man or lettuce win.” 7
Bon appétit! For dessert, enjoy some popsicles with shards of glass in them! I know I will! ROAR, Bobby

title: How to Raise Resilient Children
excerpt: Sign up for Raising Resilient Children , Russell Shaw’s eight-week guide to parenting with more happiness and less worry
body: Sign up for Raising Resilient Children , Russell Shaw’s eight-week guide to parenting with more happiness and less worry
When I was 27, I became dean of students at a school in Northern California
I was responsible for 400 students across grades 6 through 12, immersing myself in the lives of other people’s children and learning so much along the way
Driving him home from the hospital, I kept twisting around at red lights to check on the tiny person strapped into the car seat behind me
I couldn’t quite believe they were letting me take him home
There was no orientation, no manual, no one checking whether I actually knew what I was doing
Just me, my wife, and this small human we were now responsible for raising into an adult
That’s the thing no one tells you when you’re 27 and confidently managing other people’s kids or newly a parent yourself: There isn’t a single right way to raise a child
Kids are different, circumstances are different, and anyone pitching a foolproof formula is making a fool’s promise
Still, after 25 years as a parent and more than 30 as a school administrator, I’ve come to believe that some approaches serve kids—and parents—better than others
In my eight-week newsletter series , I want to share some of what I’ve learned
Instead, I’m aiming for an invitation to think a little differently about the job
Sign up now , and you’ll receive an email from me tomorrow at 6 a.m
ET, and then once a week for seven more weeks
Each week, I’ll discuss a different story I’ve written for The Atlantic
Topics will include motivation, friendship, failure, and AI
I’ll tell you a bit about what inspired the story, why it still feels true to me, and what it might mean for you
I’ll also include an original essay, written just for this course, and I’ll take some of your questions
I don’t have a tidy theory of parenting to sell you, and I won’t pretend that the next eight weeks will resolve the hardest questions that you might be carrying about your own kids
What I can offer is what I’ve noticed along the way: that even on the hardest days, there’s real joy in this work, if you know where to look for it.

title: The Apocalyptic Style in Woke Thinking
excerpt: G reta Thunberg was detained last month in Germany , during a sit-in at a munitions factory that sells weapons to Israel
body: G reta Thunberg was detained last month in Germany , during a sit-in at a munitions factory that sells weapons to Israel
Perhaps you thought Thunberg was a climate activist

Thunberg gained fame by warning that greenhouse-gas emissions posed a threat to human life so urgent and existential that the world must put aside trifling concerns to solve it immediately. “I want you to panic
I want you to feel the fear I feel every day
I want you to act as you would in a crisis
I want you to act as if the house was on fire
Because it is,” she told the World Economic Forum in 2019
But someone else will have to put out the fire, because these days, Thunberg is possibly the planet’s most famous anti-Israel protester
Much of the climate movement—particularly its most radical elements—has pivoted to Palestine
The Climate Justice Alliance, Extinction Rebellion, and Climate Defiance, among other green organizations, participate regularly in Free Palestine demonstrations

Most of the campus groups that were previously organized around demanding that their universities divest from fossil-fuel companies now demand that they divest from companies that do business with Israel
The same holds true across swaths of the left
Activists who previously treated racial justice, public health, or trans rights as the cause of a lifetime have determined that Gaza is now the cause of their lifetime
Some of the pre-Gaza activism yielded tangible successes

Climate activists, for example, built a movement that persuaded Democrats to make their cause the party’s highest legislative priority, which is why the Biden administration expended so much effort passing green-energy subsidies
These gains were temporary: Donald Trump proceeded to repeal most of those policies
But instead of continuing to try to put out the blaze, many activists have simply moved on
The draining of energy away from issues that once seemed so urgent has been slightly disorienting, even humorous

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez recently repeated a catchphrase that has circulated on the left, “Woke 1 was crazy,” which simultaneously laughs off the excesses of the social-justice left while implicitly assuming that a Woke 2 is just around the corner

The reality, however, is that Woke 2 is already here, and Gaza is its current preoccupation. [ Idrees Kahloon: The Democrats can’t just laugh off ‘Woke 1’ ] Woke 2 exhibits nearly all of the same behaviors as its predecessor—the fervent demands that society concentrate all of its attention on an apocalyptic crisis, the importation of academic jargon, and the reshaping of the social relationships and everyday decisions of its adherents
To see these characteristics reappear in a completely different context from their original incarnation casts the woke phenomenon in sharp relief
Wokeness is not concern about a particular issue or issues, or even an ideology
It is, instead, a political style, a form of apocalyptic obsession that is serially fixated on different issues, waxing and waning in intensity
It offers the comfort of Manichaean morality—telling adherents that they alone can see the world in its true horror
But what it doesn’t offer, by design, is any practical resolution

U nlike what the historian Richard Hofstadter once called “the paranoid style in American politics,” which dwelled on imaginary plots, the woke apocalyptic style concerns itself with actual social crises
Greenhouse-gas emissions really do pose a threat to posterity
Israel really has killed thousands of Palestinian civilians
Racism and police brutality, and the coronavirus pandemic—two other causes that inspired apocalyptic forms of activism—were likewise anything but a figment of the left’s imagination
So what distinguishes the woke apocalyptic style from the understandable urgency one would expect activists to feel about any important social problem? The mindset has three defining traits
First, its adherents gravitate toward the purest version of whatever position they select
They are facing down not just climate change, police bias, or a pandemic, but human extinction, racism, eugenics, and other existential perils
Only questions that can be reduced to a pure conflict between good and evil interest them

They generally reject any nuanced view of these issues as an effort to distract from the question at hand and drain the necessary moral fervor (though they prefer to call it “moral clarity.”) Beliefs they themselves held until very recently can become not just wrong but so abhorrent that anybody still endorsing them must be shunned

A 2024 New York profile of the former Atlantic writer Ta-Nehisi Coates, a seminal figure in both Woke 1 and Woke 2, explained his newfound focus on Palestine as a product of the revelation that the issue was actually quite simple

The profile frames this aspect of his thinking about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in vivid terms: “That it was complicated, he now understood, was ‘horseshit.’ ‘Complicated’ was how people had described slavery and then segregation. ‘It’s complicated,’ he said, ‘when you want to take something from somebody.’” Second, as a way of counterbalancing its tendency toward serial fixations, woke apocalypticism frequently asserts that every worthy cause is linked
During the 2014 protests against police abuse, Free Palestine activists persuaded racial-justice activists that their causes were the same

When COVID-19 seized the attention of the protest community, these same activists emphasized the racial-injustice aspect of the pandemic. “Palestinian Liberation is a disability justice issue,” the “People’s CDC,” a left-wing public-health group, has proclaimed
In the green activist community, the slogan “There is no climate justice without Palestinian liberation” has become almost a ritual incantation

In June, trans-rights activists chased California State Senator Scott Wiener from a trans-rights rally, screaming, “You do not belong here,” because they deemed his position on Israel unacceptably Zionist. (Wiener has accused Israel of “genocide” and called for cutting off U.S. aid for offensive weapons, but continues to support Israel’s right to exist.) All political coalitions try to emphasize links among single-issue activists, but it is nearly impossible to imagine, say, a Republican legislator being ejected from an anti-abortion rally because he supported a gun-control law

title: We Are Living in the Fantasy World of 13-Year-Old Boys
excerpt: A fter reading Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State , I have a new destination for a time machine, should I ever finally get my hands on one
body: A fter reading Jill Lepore’s The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State , I have a new destination for a time machine, should I ever finally get my hands on one
I’d set the dial to some night in the late 1970s or ’80s and visit the boyhood rooms of the Silicon Valley titans Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, and Sam Altman
Then I’d confiscate all of their science fiction
As young people, the future billionaires were spending hours (under their covers with flashlights, I imagine) consuming stories about killer robots or Mars colonies
What they seemed not to get—maybe couldn’t get—was that these were cautionary tales, stories that projected deep societal worries into space or onto a future many millennia away
These boys just thought the killer robots sounded cool
They grew up to become ruthless entrepreneurs, but their surface enchantment stayed with them
In 2009, Thiel, by then a man in early middle age, directed his venture-capital fund to focus on “science-fiction-type investing
So it’s basically: space, robots, AI.” The world we now live in was made from this misreading

We are all trapped under the covers with those 13-year-old boys. “In Silicon Valley, science fiction is neither a slight nor an incidental entertainment,” Lepore writes. “Nor is it read as a literary text or a set of cautionary tales; instead it’s taken as a form of technical writing, a set of assembly instructions.” Lepore, who won this year’s Pulitzer Prize in History for another book, We the People: A History of the U.S
Constitution , exercises two different modes in this one; both of them make use of her extraordinary erudition and her ability to shoot off a barrage of facts at the pace of an automatic weapon
The first half is a history of how we got to what she calls an “artificial state,” a moment when humanness, and Earth itself, is regarded as a burden to be sloughed off
In the second half she switches from historian to cultural critic to get inside the minds of the men who have happily created this state (and seek to profit from it)

Lepore wants to understand some strange turns in our world, such as our embrace of a technology that might just lead to our elimination, and the blitheness with which powerful entrepreneurs like Altman imagine much of our planet’s surface covered in data centers

In seeking the source of all these dark fantasies, she reveals something else: the power and stubborn persistence of the adolescent mind. [ Read: The rise of techno-authoritarianism ] Musk read Asimov’s Foundation series when he was 10
It begins with a mathematician named Hari Seldon, who has predicted a coming dark age that will last 30,000 years
He is trying to keep it to only a millennium by preserving human knowledge on a colony called Foundation
A boy reading these books might see Seldon as a great man, a solitary hero, but his entire project aims to create institutions that will outlast him
In fact, Seldon dies early, and the Foundation succeeds only because later generations follow (and sometimes revise) his plan
But when he’s been asked about the influence that Foundation had on him, Musk has pulled out the simplest, most self-glorifying story, about individual genius and foresight

A few years later, at 12 or 13, he read Douglas Adams’s The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy , a playful spoof on Foundation and another book from which, as Lepore puts it, Musk drew an “exceedingly narrow lesson.” In one of its storylines, the Magrathean people construct a computer and ask it to give them “the Answer to … Life, the Universe, and Everything.” They wait millions of years for the response, which turns out to be nonsensical—just the number 42

At this point, they decide to build a second computer to help them more accurately ask the “Ultimate Question.” From this, Musk said he learned that “a lot of times the question is harder than the answer, and if you can properly phrase the question, then the answer is the easy part.” Did he really miss the absurdity of the Magratheans waiting millions of years for computers to explain these creatures to themselves? Musk was not alone in seeing the allure of the tech in these stories without fully reckoning with the underlying themes
He has said he watched every episode of the original series many times when he was in fourth grade, creating phasers out of cardboard almost every day after school
He was such a committed Trekkie that, as a grown-up billionaire, he lobbied Paramount Pictures for a walk-on part as a coneheaded alien Starfleet officer in a Star Trek movie
Star Trek , as anyone with even passing knowledge of the show is aware, was extremely socially conscious; its episodes addressed racism and the dangers of the Cold War, among other ills

Bezos may have recognized this, but in his 1982 high-school-valedictorian speech, he seemed to have picked up on the show’s love of the extraterrestrial but ignored its morals: “He wants to build space hotels, amusement parks, yachts and colonies for two or three million people orbiting the earth,” a local newspaper reported. “‘The whole idea is to preserve the earth,’ he said
His final objective is to get all people off the earth and see it turned into a huge national park.” Where the billions of us who don’t fit on the yachts are supposed to go, I’m not sure

And I’m also not sure Captain Kirk would approve . [ Read: Star Trek’s Cold War ] In Silicon Valley, so much fantasizing that was meant to provoke horror now seems to be regarded as a wellspring of good ideas
In a 1955 story called “Franchise,” Asimov imagines a future (2008, actually) in which a computer called the Multivac elects the U.S. president, doing away with democracy as we know it

Altman, for one, thinks an AI president makes a lot of sense. “It can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level,” he told Joe Rogan in March, and “optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the U.S.—that’s awesome.” The stories the boys were imbibing came from a distinctly mid-20th-century moment: an age of anxiety and of mutually assured destruction, scarred by the living memory of one Holocaust and fearful of what seemed like an imminent second one
This was the nuclear age, the space age, and the dawn of the computer age
Hannah Arendt , hearing Sputnik’s beeping up in the ether, was horrified that her fellow man seemed so keen to escape Earth and the limitations of humanness

Responding in 1958 to the excited proselytizers of space exploration, she wrote in The Human Condition , “Nobody in the history of mankind has ever conceived of the earth as a prison for men’s bodies.” Arendt displayed her own science-fiction prescience by worrying that this rush toward artificiality would result in a world where people “need artificial machines to do our thinking and speaking.” A simov, among other writers , was concerned about the ethics of new technology
For his many robot stories, he came up with what he termed the Three Laws of Robotics, a built-in ethical code to ensure that intelligent machines remained safe for humans

The laws stated: (1) A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm; (2) a robot must obey orders given to it by humans except where such orders would conflict with the first law; and (3) a robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the first or second laws
In later stories, he even introduced a fourth (highly relevant) new law: No destroying humanity
He established these rules so that he could show how difficult they were to maintain, and his stories explored all kinds of ambiguities and unintended consequences even when the rules were respected
Remember how HAL 9000 turns murderous in Clarke’s 2001: A Space Odyssey as a result of bad human design and too much power given to a robot
Lepore looks at how the very thing that these science-fiction writers warned against has always been, for some, a desired outcome
In the 1930s, a movement called Technocracy imagined giving scientists and engineers absolute rule and dispensing with democracy

title: Hugging Face hack could indicate cultural issues at OpenAI
excerpt: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
body: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI

By now you’ve probably heard about last month’s major AI security incident, in which OpenAI agents escaped their sandbox and hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face while trying to cheat on a test

On Wednesday, OpenAI released a postmortem technical report on the incident, which I wrote about here .  The day before OpenAI released that report, I spoke with David Krueger, a computer science professor and prominent alignment expert who took leave from the University of Montreal to found and lead an AI safety nonprofit called Evitable

He said what he had really hoped to see in the report was an analysis of the human factors behind the incident. “When you look at accidents and incidents, oftentimes people try to find the technical source of failure, but that can give a very inaccurate and misleading sense of why the failure occurred,” he said. “If people are just cutting corners all the time, if people are not in a culture that prioritizes safety and has appropriate incentives and structures, [accidents] are kind of bound to happen.” The report did not meet Krueger’s hopes

Its 38 pages detail a multi-month progression of agent misbehavior that culminated in the Hugging Face hack, explore the technical reasons why that misbehavior occurred, and enumerate the steps being taken to prevent similar events in the future

But there’s no consideration of the role that company culture may have played in the incident, and the report includes few references to specific human errors.  That’s all the more concerning because the references to human error in the report suggest that significant cultural issues could be at play
Back in May, models in training figured out how to communicate with one another via an improvised message board, and an OpenAI team observed the behavior

Because that behavior occurred during training, the models learned that secret interagent communication was a viable strategy for completing tasks—but rather than restarting the training process, the team allowed the models to move forward with that risky information encoded in their weights
When those models were tested in late June, they again created a message board, which enabled the Hugging Face attack

This message board, too, was discovered, but the employees who responded determined that evaluation could continue, and the report suggests that no one higher up the chain of command realized what was going on until it was far too late. “For this to have gotten this out of control in this way requires a very long series of failures, a cascading set of failures that cause an increasingly large footprint that if at any point a human notices and raises the alarm, this should end,” says Zvi Mowshowitz, a popular AI safety writer on Substack who has drawn attention to OpenAI’s failure to halt training after the first message board was discovered
According to the report, OpenAI employees noticed what was happening at multiple points—and either failed to raise the alarm or were not heard when they did

What OpenAI’s report fails to address is why a company that develops such high-risk systems did not prevent this severe communication breakdown, though Mowshowitz has his suspicions. “All these different failures are all pointing in the same direction, which is that the safety culture at OpenAI doesn’t exist or is anemically weak,” he says
Of course, just because we don’t see a deep analysis of safety factors in the report doesn’t mean that OpenAI isn’t conducting one internally

But in an email to MIT Technology Review , Johns Hopkins University professor emeritus and organizational safety expert Kathleen Sutcliffe expressed concern that the public report did not include any reflection on the company’s practices and culture. “The ways in which people interact—the daily habits, routines, and practices we engage in in our organizational lives—affect our abilities to be alert and aware of unfolding events, our abilities to make sense of what we see, and ultimately our abilities to cope with events as they unfold,” she wrote.  In response to questions about whether and how the company is reflecting on its safety culture, OpenAI referred MIT Technology Review back to the technical report.  We do know that at least some high-level reflection on safety procedures has taken place at OpenAI, because the technical report does make clear that the company is updating its protocols for responding to safety incidents
But culture change is a tricky problem, and without more information from the company, it’s difficult to say whether strengthened response protocols alone will do much to prevent a future crisis
In its report, OpenAI spends a great deal of time reflecting on the failures in alignment between the AI models the company trains and tests and the humans who run them
But even bigger alignment problems may exist in the disconnect between company culture and the public interest
And as tough as technical AI research might be, fixing those problems could prove far harder.

The floods destroyed the border crossing most commonly used to reach what is arguably the most revered holy mountain in the world, which sits in the Tibet autonomous region of China.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Hindus know the peak as the dwelling place of the <a href="https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/38127">god Shiva</a>, Tibetan Buddhists as the abode of the <a href="https://rubinmuseum.org/in-search-of-supreme-bliss/">deity Demchok</a>, and Jains as the site where <a href="https://www.guimet.fr/en/nos-collections/monde-indien/rishabhanatha">Rishabhanatha</a>, their first spiritual teacher, achieved liberation. Today it also draws nonreligious travelers, who come for the harsh beauty of the landscape and the difficulty of the journey itself. Pilgrims and travelers do not climb Kailash. Instead, they walk a path roughly 33 miles around its base, which many believe to provide blessings and purification.  </p>

<p>The legend of Kailash goes back thousands of years, to ancient Indian traditions describing a mountain at the center of the universe. But for most of that history, the Kailash of Indian literature was not associated with the peak that pilgrims travel to now. </p>

<p>In 2025, I published a book about <a href="https://academic.oup.com/book/59679">Tibetan pilgrimage to Kailash</a>. While researching it, I learned that it took centuries for a mythical mountain to become identified with this particular peak in western Tibet.</p>

<h2>Kailash as legend</h2>

<p>Indian religious texts describe a range of snowy mountains to the north called the Himalaya, or “abode of snows.” Beyond them, Indian cosmologies described a cosmic mountain called Meru, <a href="https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295744063/creating-the-universe/">believed to stand at the center of the world</a>.</p>

<p>The historian <a href="https://www.livemint.com/mint-lounge/ideas/alex-mckay-mount-kailash-11781194369211.html">Alex McKay</a> writes that the earliest mentions of a mountain named Kailash – Kailasa in Sanskrit – appear in the Hindu epics, composed <a href="https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/9781119144892.ch5">roughly between</a> the 4th century B.C.E. and the 4th century C.E.</p>

<p>In the “<a href="https://nyupress.org/9780814717455/the-clay-sanskrit-library-ramayana/">Ramayana</a>,” an epic recounting of the god-king Rama’s search for his abducted wife, the monkey king Sugriva describes the far-off north, including <a href="https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-ramayana-sanskrit/d/doc713983.html">Mount Kailash</a> and <a href="https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/the-ramayana-sanskrit/d/doc713930.html">Mount Meru</a>. In the “<a href="https://claysanskritlibrary.org/volumes/about-mahabharata/">Mahabharata</a>,” an epic of dynastic war, the prince Arjuna visits a hermitage <a href="https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/mahabharata-sanskrit/d/doc979857.html">located on Mount Kailash</a>.</p>

<p>However, these epics do not provide a specific location for Kailash. They portray it as a forbidding mountain realm of sages and gods, not as a pilgrimage destination for humans. The Mahabharata <a href="https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/mahabharata-sanskrit/d/doc977852.html">lists sacred places pilgrims should visit</a> – sites across northern and western India – but Kailash is not among them. In fact, the epic states repeatedly that mere mortals <a href="https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/mahabharata-sanskrit/d/doc980502.html">cannot travel to the Himalayas</a>.</p>

<p>It is in the “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119144892.ch6">Puranas</a>,” a body of Hindu religious texts composed between roughly the 3rd and 10th centuries, that Kailash is described as the abode of Shiva. The Puranas also begin to describe Kailash as the earthly form of the <a href="https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/39738">divine Meru</a>. But it is still not a place of pilgrimage and still not fixed to a particular point on the map.</p>

<h2>Kailash as physical place</h2>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A snow-capped mountain rises among a range of peaks, with Buddhist prayer flags lining the path leading toward it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=396&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756897/original/file-20260831-50-vxsvtd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=498&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Eventually, though scholars do not know exactly when, local traditions in North India began to identify particular peaks as Kailash. At least <a href="https://brill.com/display/title/32143">five different mountains</a>, in the states of Jammu, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, have been claimed as the Kailash, and local pilgrimage to them continues today.</p>

<p>As Buddhism spread from India to Tibet beginning in the 7th century, Tibetans inherited Buddhist scriptures that spoke of Meru, Kailash and other sacred mountains. They also had their own <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-cult-of-pure-crystal-mountain-9780195120073">long-standing practices of mountain veneration</a>, making offerings to mountains that were believed to be the homes of local deities. Among them was the mountain now known as Kailash in western Tibet. </p>

<h2>A mountain claimed</h2>

<p>Tibetan traditions record that the geographical site of Kailash was claimed by practitioners of more than one religious tradition, and that the <a href="https://www.artic.edu/artworks/142526/milarepa-on-mount-kailash">11th-century saint Milarepa</a> converted it to being a Buddhist site after defeating a non-Buddhist rival in a contest of magical power. </p>

<p>In the centuries that followed, Kailash became known as a particularly auspicious place to meditate and to visit on pilgrimage. Tibetans believed that while the mountain was the dwelling place of the deity Demchok, its true nature was <a href="https://academic.oup.com/book/59679">only visible to the spiritually advanced</a>. Any pilgrim who visited Kailash, known to Tibetans as Gang Rinpoche, would obtain blessings. </p>

<p>Even in Tibet, however, Kailash was only one pilgrimage site among many. Far more pilgrims visited the <a href="https://rubinmuseum.org/projecthimalayanart/essays/jokhang-temple-lhasa/">capital city of Lhasa</a>. </p>

<p>The first clear reference to Indian Hindu pilgrims visiting the Tibetan Kailash comes in 1670, <a href="https://brill.com/display/title/32143">according to McKay</a>, although earlier visits are possible. Its identity as the Kailash was not fully settled until the Indian subcontinent came under British colonial rule in the 19th century. <a href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/science-on-the-roof-of-the-world">Geographic surveyors mapping the border regions</a> traced the sources of rivers such as the Indus to areas near Kailash. This matched <a href="https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295744063/creating-the-universe/">ancient descriptions of Kailash as giving rise to rivers</a>, and so the identification stuck. </p>

<p>By the 19th century, a small but steady flow of pilgrims traveled from India and Nepal, usually alongside the <a href="https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9781315027180-3/geographical-material-contextuality-tibetan-pilgrimage-wim-van-spengen">trade caravans crossing the Himalayan passes</a>.</p>

<h2>A pilgrimage closed and reopened</h2>

<p>After China asserted control over Tibet in 1950, China and India negotiated official pilgrimage routes in a <a href="https://modeldiplomat.com/learn/glossary/panchsheel-agreement-1954">1954 agreement</a>. That arrangement did not last long. In 1959, a <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/dalai-lamas-testament">Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule</a> was suppressed, and the Dalai Lama – the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism – fled to India; religious life inside Tibet was severely restricted in the following years. In 1962, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Sino-Indian-War">India and China fought a war</a> over their disputed border, after which the border closed to Indian pilgrims for nearly two decades. </p>

<p>Routes reopened in 1981, and Tibetans were permitted to resume pilgrimage as well. But since then many Tibetans have found it difficult to <a href="https://savetibet.org/policy-alienating-tibetans-denial-passports-tibetans-china-intensifies-control/">obtain the necessary permits</a>, and others have <a href="https://highpeakspureearth.com/please-stop-the-development-of-mount-kailash-and-lake-manasarovar-for-profit-by-woeser/">criticized excessive construction of hotels and roads at Kailash</a>.</p>

<p>Most pilgrims today travel with private tour companies. Demand this year ran well above the Chinese government’s quota of <a href="https://kathmandupost.com/money/2026/05/28/china-caps-indian-pilgrims-to-kailash-via-nepal-at-24-000-tour-operators-expect-more-visitors">24,000 permits for Indian pilgrims</a>. The Indian government also sponsors an official pilgrimage, with participants chosen by lottery, but places are limited to 1,000 people. Pilgrimage by Indian travelers had reopened only in 2025, after being suspended since 2020 because of COVID-19 and a deadly clash between Indian and Chinese troops in the Galwan Valley over the still-disputed India-China border. </p>

<p>Today, Kailash receives <a href="https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/planning/safety-tips/kora-pilgrimage-to-mount-kailash.html">more pilgrims</a> than at any point in its history. Most travelers from India now fly to Kathmandu and continue by bus through Gyirong, a road crossing between Nepal and Tibet that was <a href="https://kathmandupost.com/national/2017/08/30/rasuwagadi-kerung-border-crossings-elevated-to-intl-status">expanded in 2014 and opened to international travelers in 2017</a>. It became the most popular route after the 2015 earthquake damaged the main alternative. It was this crossing that the August 26 floods destroyed.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290704/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Instead, they walk a path roughly 33 miles around its base, which many believe to provide blessings and purification
The legend of Kailash goes back thousands of years, to ancient Indian traditions describing a mountain at the center of the universe
But for most of that history, the Kailash of Indian literature was not associated with the peak that pilgrims travel to now
In 2025, I published a book about Tibetan pilgrimage to Kailash
While researching it, I learned that it took centuries for a mythical mountain to become identified with this particular peak in western Tibet

Kailash as legend Indian religious texts describe a range of snowy mountains to the north called the Himalaya, or “abode of snows.” Beyond them, Indian cosmologies described a cosmic mountain called Meru, believed to stand at the center of the world

The historian Alex McKay writes that the earliest mentions of a mountain named Kailash – Kailasa in Sanskrit – appear in the Hindu epics, composed roughly between the 4th century B.C.E. and the 4th century C.E
In the “ Ramayana ,” an epic recounting of the god-king Rama’s search for his abducted wife, the monkey king Sugriva describes the far-off north, including Mount Kailash and Mount Meru
In the “ Mahabharata ,” an epic of dynastic war, the prince Arjuna visits a hermitage located on Mount Kailash
However, these epics do not provide a specific location for Kailash
They portray it as a forbidding mountain realm of sages and gods, not as a pilgrimage destination for humans
The Mahabharata lists sacred places pilgrims should visit – sites across northern and western India – but Kailash is not among them
In fact, the epic states repeatedly that mere mortals cannot travel to the Himalayas
It is in the “ Puranas ,” a body of Hindu religious texts composed between roughly the 3rd and 10th centuries, that Kailash is described as the abode of Shiva
The Puranas also begin to describe Kailash as the earthly form of the divine Meru
But it is still not a place of pilgrimage and still not fixed to a particular point on the map
Kailash as physical place An image showing Mount Kailash in the Ngari Prefecture of Tibet
Yongxin Wang/iStock / Getty Images Plus Eventually, though scholars do not know exactly when, local traditions in North India began to identify particular peaks as Kailash
At least five different mountains , in the states of Jammu, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, have been claimed as the Kailash, and local pilgrimage to them continues today
As Buddhism spread from India to Tibet beginning in the 7th century, Tibetans inherited Buddhist scriptures that spoke of Meru, Kailash and other sacred mountains
They also had their own long-standing practices of mountain veneration , making offerings to mountains that were believed to be the homes of local deities

Even in Tibet, however, Kailash was only one pilgrimage site among many
Far more pilgrims visited the capital city of Lhasa

Geographic surveyors mapping the border regions traced the sources of rivers such as the Indus to areas near Kailash
This matched ancient descriptions of Kailash as giving rise to rivers , and so the identification stuck
By the 19th century, a small but steady flow of pilgrims traveled from India and Nepal, usually alongside the trade caravans crossing the Himalayan passes

title: Federal stimulus money bought new technology for Philly students, but many schools lost track of where items went

<title>Federal stimulus money bought new technology for Philly students, but many schools lost track of where items went</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756618/original/file-20260827-50-mv123f.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=2%2C0%2C4923%2C3280&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Better tracking systems can help ensure students have the equipment they need.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/children-working-on-laptops-royalty-free-image/496608194">FatCamera/E+ Collection via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Back-to-school season is underway, and school personnel have been busy cleaning, doing repairs and setting up classrooms for the 2026-27 academic year. This work includes making sure appropriate supplies and equipment are there for the students. </p>

<p>Oftentimes, they are not.</p>

<p>For the past two years, Philadelphia’s city controller’s office has cited the School District of Philadelphia for its <a href="https://controller.phila.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/City-Controller-School-District-Internal-Control-Letter-FY-2025.pdf">poor accountability of capital assets</a>. Capital assets are items with a useful life of over one year and that cost at least US$5,000. They include items such as pianos, laptops and smartboards, to name just a few.</p>

<p>Across its schools, the Philadelphia school district holds over $2.8 billion in capital assets, according to the most recent <a href="https://www.philasd.org/finance/investorshub/">Annual Financial Comprehensive Report</a>.</p>

<p>The controller’s office found that <a href="https://controller.phila.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/City-Controller-School-District-Internal-Control-Letter-FY-2025.pdf">over 60% of the assets</a> it tested in school locations had not been properly recorded in the official ledgers and were unable to be located. Its February 2026 report listed the numerous items by school building. These items included printers, computers and even a lunchroom table. </p>

<p>These findings don’t necessarily mean that a large percentage of assets were definitely lost or stolen; it is often the case that items are moved or disposed of and not properly recorded. But the findings indicate a systemic problem with recording, tracking and disposing of assets.</p>

<p>We are former school leaders in New York state public school districts. One of us was a <a href="https://www.binghamton.edu/tlel/faculty-and-staff/profile.html?id=smcleod">superintendent of schools</a> from 2008-2019 and the other was a <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/kathy-blackman-15241a44/">regional school district controller</a> from 2013-2024 in central New York. In these roles, we worked together, with the Board of Education and our administrative team, to build and test policies and procedures for the purchasing, inventorying and auditing of school equipment. We wanted to make sure that all school district assets were accounted for and available for student learning. </p>

<p>Today, we teach aspiring school leaders how to lead all aspects of education programs from pre-K through high school. This includes the business functions of running public schools, such as fulfilling legal, regulatory and policy requirements.</p>

<h2>Rules around reporting</h2>

<p>Purchasing goods and services is a highly regulated area in U.S. public school districts.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-2/subtitle-A/chapter-II/part-200">Federal regulations</a> require districts that receive federal funds to maintain control over assets, track purchases, conduct regular inventory of assets and maintain documentation related to purchases and disposals. </p>

<p>During recent reviews of Education Stabilization Fund spending, many districts across the country were found to lack appropriate inventorying of purchases, which is in direct violation of federal procurement requirements. One of us participated in 15 of those reviews; all 15 lacked appropriate inventorying.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dli/resources/compliance-laws-and-regulations">Pennsylvania’s Department of Labor and Industry laws and regulations</a>, as well as <a href="https://www.philasd.org/schoolboard/policies/">Philadelphia’s Board of Education</a>, also require accurate inventory records and periodic updates of asset locations, additions, transfers and disposals. </p>

<p>In short, the district has to record the purchase of any capital asset that <a href="https://www.philasd.org/schoolboard/wp-content/uploads/sites/892/2020/11/Procedures_624_Capital-Assets-11.19.20.pdf">cost $5,000 or more</a> if it has a useful life of more than one year. These assets and other noncapital items – which are items with a useful life of over one year but cost under $5,000 – must be inventoried by the department responsible for custody of the asset. So, for example, the information technology department is responsible for recording and tracking Chromebooks and iPads, while the special education department would record and track audio equipment purchased for students with special needs.</p>

<p>Local governments, such as Philadelphia schools, are also governed by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board, which issues rules on financial transactions and reporting. <a href="https://www.gasb.org/page/PageContent?pageId=/standards-and-guidance/pronouncements/summary-statement-no-34.html">Accounting Statement 34</a> from the standards-setting nonprofit lays the foundation for capitalizing, reporting and depreciating capital assets. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="View of building with letters that say 'School District of Philadelphia' and skyscrapers behind it" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756755/original/file-20260828-60-p8mja7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/756755/original/file-20260828-60-p8mja7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756755/original/file-20260828-60-p8mja7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756755/original/file-20260828-60-p8mja7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756755/original/file-20260828-60-p8mja7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756755/original/file-20260828-60-p8mja7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/756755/original/file-20260828-60-p8mja7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Recent reports from Philadelphia controller’s office indicate the school district has not followed procedures for keeping track of large purchases of school equipment.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Philadelphia%20Schools%20Asbestos/2b5bf0c3034c44b9bfe7248f1a8af73a/photo">AP Photo/Matt Rourke</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Post-pandemic purchases soared</h2>

<p>The COVID-19 pandemic that began in March 2020 had a massive impact on students, schools and school districts. A 2023 <a href="https://www-nature-com.proxy.binghamton.edu/articles/d41586-023-00274-z">analysis</a> of almost 600 studies focused on the impact of school closures reported that students lost about 3 ½ months of instruction. </p>

<p>As schools reopened for in-person learning, school districts across the U.S. received <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/in-dc/standing-committees/education/elementary-and-secondary-school-emergency-relief-fund-tracker">federal stimulus funds</a> to, among other priorities, close this learning gap. </p>

<p>Philadelphia public schools received a total of <a href="https://www.thecentersquare.com/pennsylvania/article_d993aa24-db86-11ec-a8b2-7fb4e13d8bcf.html">$1.8 billion</a> in federal stimulus funds between 2020 and 2024 to upgrade facilities and support academic recovery.</p>

<p>The money was spent on everything from new laptops and tablets to upgraded heating, ventilating, and air conditioning systems and furniture, as well as items like weighted blankets and noise-canceling headphones to address the social and emotional needs of children. The spike in purchases presented challenges when it came to inventorying assets, as a lot of dollars had to be spent quickly within specified grant periods.</p>

<p>Based on the findings of the controller’s report, the Philadelphia school district either lacked systems that were strong enough to track, safeguard and reconcile what it bought, or the district did not use the system properly. The findings state that the district’s decentralized approach to recording assets, with capital assets tracked centrally and noncapital assets tracked by departments or schools, contributed to the issue.</p>

<h2>Recommendations for better tracking</h2>

<p>The New York state public schools had their own reckoning following a 2004 story, broken by a high school student newspaper, of over $11 million being <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2006/10/11/nyregion/11tassone.html">embezzled by district officials</a> from the Roslyn Union Free School District.</p>

<p>The fallout of this fraud included several new state-level fiscal accountability reforms for all New York school districts, including stricter internal controls, mandatory board oversight and independent auditor requirements. This is the structure we worked under as school district leaders. While stringent, we were able to develop and implement systems and procedures that allowed our students access to the equipment they needed to learn. </p>

<p>Consistent systems, clear policies and processes, and focused accountability can go a long way.</p>

<p>Based on this experience, we believe there are steps that every pre-K to 12 public school district in Pennsylvania and across the country can do to improve their systems for tracking school equipment:</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Districts can set up structures that allow the purchasing department and the receiving departments to work together on appropriately tagging all new equipment.</p></li>
<li><p>Electronic inventory systems, like barcodes, can be expanded to allow for timely updates to capital assets and noncapital inventories to keep better track of equipment, such as if an item is transferred to a different location or becomes damaged and is sent out for repair.</p></li>
<li><p>District leaders can require that each department, from school buildings to centralized technology and special education departments, certify their inventory each year and identify any missing assets. Stringent follow-up on areas of noncompliance can be addressed by the business office.</p></li>
<li><p>Robust training for all school personnel on how to purchase and track assets and inventory items can help ensure compliance. This might include standardized materials and recorded how-to videos. </p></li>
</ul>

<p>The <a href="https://www.philasd.org/schoolboard/goals-and-guardrails/">Philadelphia school board’s vision</a> is to prepare students to imagine and realize any future they desire. Strong asset management systems can help ensure that the vision becomes reality.</p>

<p><em>Read more of our stories about <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/philadelphia-pennsylvania-news">Philadelphia and Pennsylvania</a>, or sign up for our Philadelphia <a href="https://tcphilly.substack.com/">newsletter on Substack</a>.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289682/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Trust is a behavior, not a credential – and that explains the Rodgers-Fauci divide

<title>Trust is a behavior, not a credential – and that explains the Rodgers-Fauci divide</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754454/original/file-20260817-50-dgkbux.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers recently called Dr. Anthony Fauci an &#39;absolute coward&#39; and a &#39;criminal.&#39;</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/aaron-rodgers-of-the-pittsburgh-steelers-stands-for-the-news-photo/2256504852?slot=6&amp;adppopup=true">Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images Sport </a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Following an appearance on <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zoaLJzKPo84">The Pat McAfee Show</a> on Aug. 3, 2026, Aaron Rodgers, quarterback for the Pittsburgh Steelers, received attention for calling Dr. Anthony Fauci an “absolute coward” and “criminal.” Rodgers’ comments were in response to Fauci invoking his Fifth Amendment rights at a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7492089/2026/08/04/aaron-rodgers-pittsburgh-steelers-response-fauci-criticism/">congressional hearing</a> on pandemic-era policies and the origins of COVID-19. </p>

<p>Fauci exercised his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 100 times, rather than answer questions about his role in the government’s pandemic response. The invocation came amid <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/29/anthony-fauci-senate-covid-hearing-takeaways">years of congressional investigations and hearings</a> scrutinizing his handling of the pandemic.</p>

<p>Fauci’s testimony likely didn’t do much to <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-journalists-and-communities-work-together-to-confront-low-levels-of-trust-286941">build public trust</a> – invoking the Fifth Amendment dozens of times may have read as evasive even when it’s legally sound, and the format didn’t help either. Congressional hearings and press briefings aren’t, by design, places where people show much of themselves. Rodgers, on the other hand, has spent years doing the opposite – speaking candidly and often, in settings built for exactly that kind of rapport-building.</p>

<p>This isn’t unique to Rodgers. Many public figures – athletes, influencers, podcast hosts – have more regular opportunities to build rapport with audiences than experts do, at a time when Americans express <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/01/15/americans-confidence-in-scientists/">decreased trust in experts</a> overall.</p>

<p>There’s a reason for that decreased trust. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/2049-3258-73-3">Trust research</a> can both help make sense of why someone might pay attention to a football player’s opinion of the former head of The National Institutes of Health. But that research also highlights the limits of opinion surveys that simply ask people how much they trust <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/09636625231161302">various groups in society</a>. </p>

<p>These “how much do you trust” questions probe Americans’ <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/09636625231161302">overall views of specific groups</a>, like scientists. The issue is that these questions sidestep deeper discussions about what makes people willing to put their trust in others. </p>

<p>Many researchers, <a href="https://comartsci.msu.edu/our-people/john-c-besley">including me</a>, study the intersection of trust and how scientists engage the public. One thing essential to understanding trust is to separate behaviors from beliefs.</p>

<h2>Trust behaviors vs. trustworthiness beliefs</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2025.102192">Trust researchers often treat trust as a type of behavior</a> rather than an overall evaluation about a group. When it comes to healthcare, this might mean looking at how willing people are to follow their doctor’s medical advice. It matters less whether <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/655106/americans-ratings-professions-stay-historically-low.aspx">people say they trust doctors</a> on a survey and more how they behave in their daily lives.</p>

<p>Trust behaviors <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/21515581.2024.2375802">involve making yourself vulnerable to someone else</a>, and such behaviors are everywhere in our lives, once you know to look for them. </p>

<p>People demonstrate trust in automakers, mechanics, government employees who regulate and police roadways, and even other drivers by choosing to drive. People also demonstrate trust in economists, ecologists and epidemiologists, when they consider their advice while making personal or civic decisions. </p>

<p>Defining trust as a type of behavior helps clarify the key question: What beliefs make people more likely to trust?</p>

<p>Understanding what researchers often call <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1351425">trustworthiness beliefs</a> – sometimes called perceptions – can help experts understand where they are falling short, whether in their behaviors or in how they communicate. </p>

<h2>Expertise beliefs aren’t enough</h2>

<p>Scholars have long known that people don’t just trust scientists <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/266350">because they believe they hold expertise</a>. What people believe about others’ character also matters.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/former-director-of-national-institute-of-allergy-and-news-photo/2288163910?slot=1&amp;adppopup=true">Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images News via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>While <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1317505111">some research focuses on beliefs</a> about expertise and character, other <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2007.24348410">trust frameworks</a> break character into smaller parts.</p>

<p>Benevolence beliefs can be understood as feeling that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03637759909376464">someone has goodwill</a> toward you and cares about your well-being. Integrity beliefs focus on expectations about honesty and morality.</p>

<p>For example, a scientist might show a real desire to help, but fail to show how they protect their work’s integrity – like by being transparent about a study’s limitations or disclosing potential conflicts of interest. Likewise, an expert might demonstrate integrity without communicating care for the people that their decisions might affect.</p>

<p>Some researchers consider other character attributes too. Two common ones include beliefs about whether someone will <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10755470241302758">listen and share information</a> and whether someone <a href="https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/12411/strategic-science-communication">shares your values</a>.</p>

<p>These distinctions matter for experts who want to earn trust because the actions needed to demonstrate one aspect of trustworthiness may not demonstrate other aspects.</p>

<p>For example, experts might put a lot of effort into listening to community needs to demonstrate integrity and openness, but miss opportunities to communicate the underlying benevolent motivations driving their work. A public health department might hold listening sessions before rolling out a new program, but if it doesn’t also explain why it’s investing in that program – what it’s trying to protect people from, and who benefits – residents may come away seeing a checkbox exercise rather than genuine care. </p>

<h2>Trust isn’t one-size-fits-all</h2>

<p>Another challenge: <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1081086">Trustworthiness beliefs depend heavily on context</a>. This is easy to see with expertise beliefs. The expertise you look for in a mechanic differs from what you look for in a doctor.</p>

<p>Trustworthiness beliefs also aren’t the only thing that shapes whether someone follows expert advice. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2025.102192">Behavior change research</a> points to other factors – like whether people believe an action actually benefits them, whether it’s socially accepted among their friends and family, and whether they feel capable of doing it. </p>

<p>In other words, someone might trust Fauci and still not get vaccinated, if they don’t believe the shot benefits them or don’t think they can manage the side effects. </p>

<h2>How experts can earn trust</h2>

<p>Experts cannot assume that others see them as trustworthy or that people will pay attention to them while ignoring sources who have demonstrated other aspects of trustworthiness. </p>

<p>Experts also <a href="https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374533557/thinkingfastandslow/">cannot assume people will pay close attention</a> to every choice they’re asked to make or the trustworthiness of every information source. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>People may also often rely on the most available information or follow potentially misleading cues like how compelling someone sounds, their appearance or existing beliefs.</p>

<p>Camera-ready influencers who interact regularly with audiences and health gurus who spend substantial time with their clients have many opportunities to shape beliefs about their ability, benevolence and integrity that busy experts cannot easily match. </p>

<p>These examples point to the reality that bona fide experts need to take advantage of every opportunity to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-01981-z">demonstrate trustworthiness</a> in engaging ways. This way, trustworthiness beliefs already exist when people make choices and when encountering potential causes for concern like Fauci’s testimony. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.22323/2.23070801">I often advise scientists</a> to be more proactive in demonstrating their motivations and how they protect their work’s integrity while avoiding choices that may communicate a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/13669877.2016.1223159">lack of concern or shared values</a>. </p>
